Title: Evolution of Foreign Direct Investment in the second half of 2021 Ovidio Reyes Ramrez, President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua
text: 1960 1960 Issuing confidence and stability Wednesday, March 30, 2022 Evolution of Foreign Direct Investment in the second half of 2021Ovidio Reyes Ramirez, President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua Good morning everyone. Thank you to those who are watching and listening to us through the different media and to all those present, also Companero Laureano Ortega, Investment Advisor to the Government of Nicaragua. Today we are pleased to present a report on the update and evolution of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Nicaragua for the second half of 2021. Previously, we had presented the FDI evolution report for the first half of 2021. The Central Bank of Nicaragua has been publishing reports on improvements in FDI indicators that are carried out according to comparable international standards. As we have previously pointed out, this work is carried out on the basis of the recommendations and support of international organizations that record these flows, such as the CAPTAC-DR center of the International Monetary Fund. In recent years, FDI flows in Nicaragua have been affected by different shocks and, most recently during 2020, by the global COVID-1 pandemic 9. In our records published in the 2020 Annual Report and the latest Balance of Payments report for the third quarter of 2021, the impact that the pandemic had on external flows can be seen. We are now proceeding to review and update the previous and current information, we hope that with this information that we will make available on our website, it will be accessible to the public and investors. This FDI update is carried out with data from the Quarterly Foreign Investment Survey that consults more than 270 companies with foreign capital participation, which is described below. As in the rest of the countries of the Central American region, Panama and the Dominican Republic, in 2021 Nicaragua presented a trend of economic recovery and FDI, aligned with the recovery of global economic activity. Thus, in the second half of 2021, gross FDI inflows in Nicaragua amounted to US625.3 million, 18.0 percent higher than the amount recorded in the same period of 2020 (US527.2 million). The amount of FDI inflows represented the equivalent of 8 percent of GDP in 2021 (8.1 percent in the second half of 2020). For its part, net FDI flows during the second half of 2021 totaled 500.3 million dollars, which meant an increase of 91.6 million dollars compared to the same period in 2020 (US 408.7 million). In cumulative terms, in 2021 gross FDI receipts totaled US1,470.1 million, equivalent to 10.5% of GDP, which translated into an increase of 52.7 percent compared to 2020 or US507.2 million compared to what was recorded in 2020, which accumulated US962.9 million (7.7% of GDP). This increase came mainly from the reinvestment of profits, new investments that were financed through the companies' headquarters, as well as from the recovery of income from FDI investment. Meanwhile, net FDI flows accumulated 1,220.1 million dollars, equivalent to 8.7% of GDP, reflecting a growth of 63.4 percent compared to what was observed in 2020 (US 746.5 million, 5.9% of GDP). The economic sectors with the highest net FDI flows were energy and mines, which attracted 466.5 million dollars (38.2% of the total); manufacturing industry with 263.4 million dollars equivalent to 21.6% of the total; communications with 1,74.8 million dollars, equivalent to 14.3% of the total; and trade and services with 1 46.4 million dollars, equivalent to 1 2.0% of the total. In terms of the origin of net FDI flows, in the accumulated to 2021, FDI from the United States totaled 444.3 million dollars, being 180.7 million dollars higher than in 2020 (US 263.6 million); from Canada it totaled 213.8 million dollars, which meant an increase of 122.5 million dollars compared to 2020 (US 91.3 million); Panama registered 185.2 million dollars, 90.2 million dollars higher than in 2020 (US 95.0 million); from Mexico were 167.5 million dollars, which compared to 2020 (US 110.3 million) increased by 57.2 million dollars; and finally Spain and Costa Rica totaled 108.0 and 41.8 million dollars*, respectively, being 74.6 and 31.1 million dollars higher than in 2020. As we can see, the recent strong economic recovery is also being accompanied by a similar dynamic of both gross and net FDI. Title: The National Economy during 2023 and Perspectives Remarks by the President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua, Ovidio Reyes
text: fiaenfadde Issuing confidence and stability WORDS OF THE AUTHORITIES Tuesday, December 19, 2023 The national economy during 2023 and Perspectives Remarks by the President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua, Ovidio Reyes Good morning. Comrade Gustavo Porras, President of the Honorable National Assembly, members of the board of directors, deputies and all those present. Thank you very much for inviting me to this parliamentary session to explain the recent economic evolution of our country and the prospects that we envision for 2024, from the Central Bank of Nicaragua. During 2023, the Nicaraguan economy has managed to consolidate and is currently in a stage of economic expansion. The economy has managed to recover the path of sustained economic growth in which most economic sectors show a positive evolution, to such an extent that the year will end better than expected. As of the third quarter of 2023, the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by .2 percent year-on-year while the average growth of 2023 reaches a rate of 4.5 percent, driven mainly by the activities of hotels and restaurants, mining and quarrying, electricity, transport and communications, financial intermediation, trade and construction. The boost to economic growth was driven by domestic demand, with growth in consumption and investment, which was tempered by the decline in net external demand. Correspondingly, the unemployment rate remains low and stable. The unemployment rate in October 2023 was 3.8%, accompanied by stability in formal employment and a reduction in informal employment. Thus, a recovery of formal employment has been observed by the Nicaraguan Social Security Institute, which as of November presented an affiliation of 795,924 insured persons, mainly due to increases in the services and construction sectors. Domestic inflation is slowing and expectations are anchoring at a lower level. The latter is associated with the gradual decline in international prices and a balanced national monetary and fiscal policy that have made it possible to maintain solid major financial balances. Year-on-year inflation as of November 2023 was 5.65 percent, when it ended at 11.58 percent in 2022, that is, it has slowed down by half, while accumulated inflation for the year reaches a lower rate of 3.98 percent. The positive performance of monetary variables has continued to generate room to favor economic growth. In this regard, as of November 2023, all monetary aggregates grew at double-digit rates in year-on-year terms. The foreign exchange market is very stable and there is a flow of foreign currency, which is reflected in a low exchange rate gap that has remained at around 0.3 percent during the last two years. The Central Bank has not had a demand for foreign currency from the market, but, rather, on the contrary, financial institutions have sold the Central Bank up to 1,215.3 million dollars to meet their greater demand for cordobas. This result indicates that the economy is signaling not a higher, but a lower exchange rate, which is why our institution announced an additional reduction in the exchange rate slippage, bringing it to zero percent as of January 1, 2024, when the exchange rate will stand at 36.6243 cordobas per United States Dollar and will remain so for the next year. Financial intermediation shows a positive evolution, consolidating credit growth. The dynamism of economic activity continues to have a positive impact on the expectations of economic agents and the ability of households and companies to pay. The Nicaraguan financial system continues to show a solid and resilient position, with increased profitability, as well as capital and liquidity levels above regulatory minimums. There is also a sustained reduction in the portfolio at risk and non-performing loans. This year, there has been a significant recovery in lending reflected in increases in the portfolio, mainly leveraged by higher deposits from the public. Thus, as of November 2023, credit grew 1 7.5 percent and deposits grew 1 6.5 percent, in year-on-year terms. Public sector balance sheets remain balanced, with tax revenue growth and a prudent public spending policy that has allowed for fiscal consolidation. Therefore, the result of the Non-Financial Public Sector (NFPS) reflects a surplus (after grants) in the accumulated January-September 2023, as well as in the accumulated of the last twelve months. Likewise, appropriate financing has been maintained, both from external and internal sources, while public debt has decreased in terms of GDP and stands at a sustainable level of o0.2 percent in October 2023. The monetary and fiscal performance has favored the strengthening of the BCN's Gross International Reserves (RIB). In this way, until November 2023 the reserves have increased by 956.1 million dollars, reaching a historical balance of 5,360.6 million dollars, as well as a coverage of 3.4 times the monetary base and 8 months of merchandise imports, which increases the capacity to safeguard the current exchange regime. The balance of payments as of September continues to register dynamism in external flows related to exports of goods, foreign direct investment, family remittances and tourism. However, the external context has resulted in lower demand for free zone exports, which show a reduction. At the same time, imports have decreased, mainly due to the lower oil bill and the decrease in imports of inputs by companies under the free zone regime. Thus, merchandise export revenues to October were 3,449.6 million dollars, reflecting a year-on-year growth of 3.0 percent. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) to June reached the sum of 1,447 million dollars, which represented a year-on-year growth of 28.9 percent. Accumulated family remittances through October stood at 3,844.4 million dollars, growing by 49.1 percent year-on-year. While tourism revenues to October reached 422.8 million dollars, growing year-on-year by 2.8 percent. The economic outlook for 2023 has improved and is positive for 2024, expecting dynamism to be maintained and strengthened in the medium and long term. The Central Bank is now projecting that economic growth in 2023 will be in a range of between 4.0 and 5.0 percent and that in 2024 it will be in a range of between 3.5 and 4.5 percent. These estimates are higher than originally anticipated, even as downside risks remain latent in the global economy. Inflation is expected to end in 2023 in a range of between 4.5 and 5.5 percent, subsequently converging to lower inflation of between 3.0 and 4.0 percent by 2024. While employment is expected to remain stable, with an unemployment rate of between 3.0 and 3.5 percent in 2023 and 2024. On the external sector side, the balance of payments is expected to present a current account surplus of between 4.5 and 5.5 percent of GDP by 2023 and between 3.0 and 4.0 percent of GDP by 2024. The Central Bank of Nicaragua will continue to conduct its monetary and exchange policy in accordance with international conditions and domestic monetary and financial conditions. In this way, in the short term the Central Bank will keep the Monetary Reference Rate (TRM) unchanged at 7.0 percent as long as it continues to contribute to economic stability, employment and prices, and to facilitate financial intermediation. Although we will be monitoring to adjust it in case of changes in global and local conditions. Although the outlook for 2024 is favorable, risks persist that could affect macroeconomic developments. The main risks to our economy are the materialization of shocks due to geopolitical conflicts that lead to increases in oil and food prices, the tightening of monetary policy in the main industrial economies that are struggling to contain more persistent inflation, and those related to climatic events. Even when external and climatic risks are latent, the Nicaraguan economy has developed enough strengths to mitigate them. Our country today has a dynamic and resilient export sector, greater diversification of production and trade, greater savings capacity, a solid and liquid financial system, as well as balanced and responsible fiscal, monetary and financial policies. These economic strengths can contribute to higher growth and employment and lower inflation than expected. Strengths shield the country against future adverse events and are a key condition for the continuity of economic growth and stability. In conclusion, I must acknowledge that this good macroeconomic performance is the result of appropriate government policies that have favoured markets and created the conditions for a vigorous recovery. Small, medium and large businesses have found outlets for their ventures and investments, as well as for trade, both national and international. Public policies have been key. The development of social and productive infrastructure projects has facilitated the attention and mobilization of all sectors. The different public services and promotion in all spaces is allowing us to reap these fruits that are benefiting all Nicaraguan families so much. I thank you very much for your attention and wish you all a Merry Christmas 2023 and a Happy New Year 2024. TT You Tube GerenciadeComunicaciones@bcn.gob.ni
text_original: fiaenfadde Emitiendo confianza y estabilidad PALABRAS DE LAS AUTORIDADES Martes, 19 de diciembre de 2023 La economa nacional durante 2023 y Perspectivas Palabras del Presidente del Banco Central de Nicaragua, Ovidio Reyes Buenos das. Compaero Gustavo Porras, Presidente de la honorable Asamblea Nacional, miembros de la unta directiva, diputados y todos los presentes. Muchas gracias por invitarme a esta sesin parlamentaria para explicar la evolucin econmica reciente de nuestro pas y las perspectivas que visualizamos para 2024, desde el Banco Central de Nicaragua. Durante 2023, la economa nicaragense ha logrado consolidarse y se encuentra en este momento en una etapa de expansin econmica. La economa ha logrado recuperar la senda de crecimiento econmico sostenido en el que la mayora de los sectores econmicos muestran una evolucin positiva, a tal punto que el ao finalizar mejor que lo previsto. Al tercer trimestre de 2023, el Producto Interno Bruto (PIB) creci .2 por ciento interanual mientras que el crecimiento promedio de 2023 alcanza una tasa de 4.5 por ciento, impulsado principalmente por las actividades de hoteles y restaurantes, explotacin de minas y canteras, electricidad, transporte y comunicaciones, intermediacin financiera, comercio y construccin. El impulso al crecimiento econmico estuvo determinado por la demanda interna, con crecimiento del consumo y la inversin, lo que se vio atenuado por la disminucin de la demanda externa neta. Correspondientemente, la tasa de desempleo permanece baja y estable. La tasa de desempleo en octubre de 2023 fue de 3.8%, acompaada de estabilidad en el empleo formal y reduccin en el empleo informal. As, se viene observando una recuperacin del empleo formal del Instituto Nicaragense de Seguridad Social, que a noviembre present una afiliacin de 795,924 asegurados, principalmente por aumentos en los sectores de servicios y la construccin. La inflacin domstica se est desacelerando y las expectativas se estn anclando a un nivel ms bajo. Esto ltimo se asocia con el descenso gradual de los precios internacionales y a una poltica monetaria y fiscal nacional equilibradas que han permitido mantener slidos los principales balances financieros. La inflacin interanual a noviembre de 2023 fue de 5.65 por ciento, cuando finaliz en 11.58 por ciento en 2022, es decir, se ha desacelerado en la mitad, mientras que la inflacin acumulada del ao alcanza una tasa ms baja, de 3.98 por ciento. El desempeo positivo de las variables monetarias ha seguido generando espacio para favorecer el crecimiento econmico. En este sentido, a noviembre de 2023 todos los agregados monetarios crecieron a tasas de dos dgitos en trminos interanuales. El mercado cambiario se encuentra muy estable y hay flujo de divisas, lo que se refleja en una brecha cambiara baja que se ha mantenido en alrededor del 0.3 por ciento durante los ltimos dos aos. El Banco Central no ha tenido demanda de divisas por parte del mercado, sino, ms bien, todo lo contrario, las entidades financieras han llegado a vender al Banco Central hasta 1,215.3 millones de dlares para satisfacer su mayor demanda por crdobas. Este resultado indica que la economa est sealizando no un mayor, sino un menor tipo de cambio, razn que motiv a nuestra institucin anunciar una reduccin adicional del deslizamiento cambiario llevndolo a cero por ciento a partir del primero de enero de 2024, cuando el tipo de cambio se ubicar en 36.6243 crdobas por Dlar de los Estados Unidos de Amrica y permanecer as durante el prximo ao. La intermediacin financiera muestra una evolucin positiva, consolidndose el crecimiento del crdito. El dinamismo de la actividad econmica sigue incidiendo positivamente sobre las expectativas de los agentes econmicos y la capacidad de pago de los hogares y de las empresas. El sistema financiero nicaragense contina mostrando una posicin slida y de resiliencia, con aumento de su rentabilidad, as como con niveles de capital y liquidez superiores a los mnimos regulatorios. Tambin se observa una reduccin sostenida de la cartera en riesgo y de la mora. En este ao, se ha destacado una recuperacin importante del crdito reflejada en aumentos de la cartera, apalancados principalmente por los mayores depsitos del pblico. As, a noviembre de 2023, el crdito creci 1 7.5 por ciento y los depsitos crecieron 1 6.5 por ciento, en trminos interanuales. Los balances del sector pblico se mantienen equilibrados, con crecimiento de los ingresos tributarios y una poltica prudente de gasto pblico que ha permitido una consolidacin fiscal. Por consiguiente, el resultado del Sector Pblico No Financiero (SPNF) refleja supervit (despus de donaciones) en el acumulado enero-septiembre de 2023, al igual que en el acumulado de los ltimos doce meses. As mismo, se ha mantenido un financiamiento apropiado, tanto de fuentes externas como internas, al tiempo que la deuda pblica ha disminuido en trminos del PIB y se ubica en un nivel sostenible de 0.2 por ciento en octubre de 2023. El desempeo monetario y fiscal ha favorecido el fortalecimiento de las Reservas Internacionales Brutas (RIB) del BCN. De esta forma, hasta noviembre de 2023 las reservas han aumentado en 956.1 millones de dlares, alcanzando un saldo histrico de 5,360.6 millones de dlares, as como una cobertura de 3.4 veces la base monetaria y de 8 meses de importaciones de mercancas, lo que aumenta la capacidad para resguardar el rgimen cambiario vigente. La balanza de pagos al mes de septiembre contina registrando dinamismo en los flujos externos relacionados con las exportaciones de mercancas, inversin extranjera directa, remesas familiares y turismo. No obstante, el contexto externo ha resultado en una menor demanda de exportaciones de zona franca, las que muestran una reduccin. Al mismo tiempo, las importaciones han disminuido, principalmente por la menor factura petrolera y la disminucin de importaciones de insumos de las empresas bajo el rgimen de zonas francas. De esta manera, los ingresos por exportaciones de mercancas a octubre fueron de 3,449.6 millones de dlares, reflejando un crecimiento interanual del 3.0 por ciento. La Inversin Extranjera Directa (IED) a junio alcanz la suma de 1,447 millones de dlares, lo que represent un crecimiento interanual del 28.9 por ciento. Las remesas familiares acumuladas a octubre se ubicaron en 3,844.4 millones de dlares, creciendo en 49.1 por ciento interanual. Mientras que los ingresos por turismo a octubre alcanzaron 422.8 millones de dlares, creciendo interanualmente en 2.8 por ciento. Las perspectivas econmicas para 2023 han mejorado y son positivas para 2024, esperando que se mantenga el dinamismo y ste se fortalezca en el mediano plazo y largo plazo. El Banco Central est ahora proyectando que el crecimiento econmico del 2023 se ubique en un rango de entre 4.0 y 5.0 por ciento y que en 2024 se ubique en un rango de entre 3.5 y 4.5 por ciento. Estas estimaciones son superiores a las previstas originalmente, an cuando en la economa mundial se mantienen latentes los riesgos hacia la baja. La inflacin se espera que finalice en 2023 en un rango de entre 4.5 y 5.5 por ciento, convergiendo posteriormente a una menor inflacin de entre 3.0 y 4.0 por ciento para 2024. Mientras que el empleo se prev que contine estable, con una tasa de desempleo de entre 3.0 y 3.5 por ciento en 2023 y 2024. Por el lado del sector externo, se espera que la balanza de pagos presente un supervit de cuenta corriente de entre 4.5 y 5.5 por ciento del PIB para 2023 y de entre 3.0 y 4.0 por ciento del PIB para 2024. El Banco Central de Nicaragua continuar conduciendo su poltica monetaria y cambiara en correspondencia de las condiciones internacionales y las condiciones monetarias y financieras internas. De esta manera, en el corto plazo el Banco Central mantendr invariable en 7.0 por ciento la Tasa de Referencia Monetaria (TRM) mientras sta siga contribuyendo a la estabilidad econmica, del empleo y los precios, y que facilite la intermediacin financiera. Aunque estaremos monitoreando para ajustarla en caso de ocurrir cambios en las condiciones globales y locales. Si bien las perspectivas para el ao 2024 son favorables, persisten riesgos que podran afectar la evolucin macroeconmica. Los principales riesgos de nuestra economa son la materializacin de choques por conflictos geopolticos que deriven en aumentos en los precios del petrleo y los alimentos, el endurecimiento de la poltica monetaria de las principales economas industriales que estn luchando para contener una inflacin ms persistente, y los relacionados a los eventos climticos. An cuando los riesgos externos y climticos estn latentes, la economa nicaragense ha desarrollado suficientes fortalezas para mitigarlos. Nuestro pas hoy cuenta con un sector exportador dinmico y resiliente, una mayor diversificacin de la produccin y el comercio, una mayor capacidad de ahorro, un sistema financiero slido y lquido, as como polticas fiscales, monetarias y financieras equilibradas y responsables. Estas fortalezas econmicas pueden contribuir a obtener un crecimiento y empleo superiores y una menor inflacin que la prevista. Las fortalezas blindan al pas frente a futuros acontecimientos adversos y son una condicin clave para la continuidad del crecimiento econmico y la estabilidad. Para finalizar, debo reconocer que este buen resultado macroeconmico es fruto de polticas gubernamentales apropiadas que han favorecido los mercados y creado las condiciones para que se produzca una reactivacin pujante. Los negocios pequeos, medianos y grandes han encontrado salidas para sus emprendimientos e inversiones, as como para el comercio, tanto nacional como internacional. Las polticas pblicas han sido claves. El desarrollo de proyectos de infraestructura social y productiva han facilitado la atencin y movilizacin de todos los sectores. Los diferentes servicios pblicos y la promocin en todos los espacios, est permitiendo cosechar estos frutos que tanto estn beneficiado a todas las familias nicaragenses. Agradezco mucho su atencin y les deseo a todos que tengan una Feliz Navidad 2023 y un Prspero Ao Nuevo 2024.  TT You Tube 1 GerenciadeComunicaciones@bcn.gob.ni www.bcn.gob.ni

Title: Transcript of the words of the President of the BCN at the VII Business Forum: Perspective, Development and Food Security
text: TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Participation of the President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R., in the Business Forum: Perspective, Economic Development and Food Security, 2022-2026 June 29, 2022 Words from the presenter of the event: We would like to invite Ovidio Reyes, President of the Central Bank, to join us for his presentation. Economic Development and Food Security Perspectives. President of the BCN: Good morning everyone. Good morning gentlemen of the table that presides over this business activity. Well, the topic that I am going to deal with is a little different, but it has to do with the issue that you point out, it is an issue that the Minister of Finance had prepared, but he could not attend the event because of having to attend to emergencies and financial preparations. And in my case, I am going to talk to you a little about what our monetary institution evaluates, and gives continuity to, which is the economic position in which the country finds itself, the finances and prospects. Development issues are very important issues, but I do not come prepared with food security issues, nor development issues, but yes, this is important, and it has to do with it. You You You You TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION What is that growth rate? Well, it is something that we are going to monitor, evaluate; but we believe that we have the potential to keep it at around 5%; a year a little less, a few years a little more, but we have the potential to achieve it. Statistics indicate that the sectors that are currently maintaining this dynamic are related first to the export sector. The role that the primary sector has played in this economy is quite laudable and remarkable, it has been the main economic strength that we have had, it has been and has not succumbed to any event. If someone asks about risks, the primary sector of our economy is the one that bears the greatest, or the greatest disturbances, and, therefore, it is the sector with the least risk. That is a great lesson, because before many bet that it was the development of other sectors, which during the pandemic proved to have less strength and succumbed to shocks, but the primary sector did not. And when I talk about the primary sector, I am referring to agriculture, the livestock sector, the mining production sector, fisheries and aquaculture and the forestry sector. Contradictorily, in many of the analyses that were made prior to the shocks by scholars of the subject and international organizations, they all spoke of a backward primary and agricultural sector. All those stories that we heard of weakness, etcetera, etcetera, and they put other sectors as the leading sectors of development. Well, that was an analysis that did not take into account that the economy suffers from these disturbances. Now that they happened, that is history of the past, it is really where we must bet, it is where we must bet because it is also closely linked to the outside and what is no longer sold here is sold abroad, period. So, I think that Nicaragua did a lot to put its main energies there, because now they are serving us as a fundamental bastion, as the backbone of the economy. It has kept the flow going TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION If there is one thing we have to bet on, it is to continue strengthening productivity in this sector, to continue generating training, to continue generating education, to continue providing technologies that have really done the work of guaranteeing Nicaragua's food and also to guarantee financing and the flow of foreign currency for the rest of the sectors. Of course, at the moment they are being favored by an improvement in international prices, which the question is whether it will be sustained? From what has happened with inflation, it seems that we are in a new state of prices. That is, many of these products are not likely to return to previous prices, some of them, including energy prices. Perhaps a great energy revolution would have to come to drive down prices, but the truth is that demand exists for all goods and, therefore, it is very unlikely that there will be a generalized drop in the prices of the products that we export. This has pros and cons because this price chain is transmitted to the domestic economy and also affects consumer prices, but, as some think, it is better to have good prices than bad prices. It is better to have good prices that stimulate and encourage production than to have bad prices, so that there is no economic activity that can be encouraged or mobilized for this purpose. In terms of production, then, we have been growing at this rate of 4.7% in April and in terms of economic activity in the first quarter, it accumulated more than 5% compared to the previous year. We believe so, by the end of the year we could remain in that range between 4 and 5%. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Until now, after the socio-political crisis we lowered our reserves to 2,100 million dollars, and today we have been able to recover them to the point that we already have 4,350 million dollars of international reserves, an amount sufficient enough to continue advancing in growth and also to withstand any other eventuality that may come from the international level, but, there is no monetary imbalance, nor is there an exchange rate imbalance. There is no exchange rate imbalance in Nicaragua. The exchange rate of purchase and sale remains stable, the flow of foreign exchange sales and free convertibility is preserved. And when one goes to the fiscal accounts one observes that there is also fiscal balance, and that to date as of April there has been a fiscal surplus. So, if there is a fiscal surplus and if there is monetary balance, then why is inflation above 10%, well, because international prices skyrocketed. Our economy is open, very open. I think that today it is more open than many times ago. We are talking about a flow of exports that will perfectly reach 7 billion dollars compared to a GDP of around 13 billion dollars and imports that last year reached almost 10 billion dollars. So, it's an extremely open economy. Therefore, what happens outside has repercussions here. And if inflation driven by energy and food prices at the international level rises, it rises here. So, a lot will depend on what others do to contain inflation and how it will affect us here. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION However, there is an interest rate that we could not match. If the United States, for example, begins to raise the interest rate in a more aggressive way and what happened in the last fight against inflation in the United States happens, when interest rates exceeded double digits, we will hardly be able to compete against that interest rate. That is, the Central Bank (of Nicaragua) is not going to raise the interest rate to those levels. The best thing to do is to let the economy adjust. One can act to a certain extent, but we are not going to sacrifice much just to sustain a competition of resources, because when interest rates rise, we really start to compete all for resources. In other words, the money begins to flow to where it is most profitable. And if they are paying you a very good interest rate outside, why are you going to have it inside? Ok! But hey, these are things that are pending to be seen. For now, we have had the capacity to maintain balances with our policy and with our adjustments in the interest rate, which we have been gradually increasing until it is now 5%, and we believe that we could continue and continue on that trajectory. Regarding employment. Employment has recovered, it is observed that formal employment in the INSS has been increasing steadily and the unemployment rate has been falling. The problem is that the unemployment rate, although it measures a reduction, does not measure the labor participation component, what does that mean? The participation of the population in the labor force, which is what puts pressure on wages, from there is that the unemployment rate is measured, not on the total economically active population, well, there have been many people who for multiple reasons have withdrawn from labor participation, and that is also a global phenomenon, and they have not returned to the labor market. Many factors can have an impact on that, we have been doing analyses, but it is very difficult. One of them is that many people dedicated themselves to activities more at home, less exposed to pandemic issues, but also TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION How to deal with inflation? As I said, being an external phenomenon, then we as a nation cannot confront it directly, because that would mean tightening monetary and fiscal policy a lot that could cause a recession, and we do not want that, and who knows if we can control it because it comes from outside, so we are going to wait for the actions. The most that can be done is to compensate, as the government has been doing, with support and subsidy policies to alleviate its effects. However, we have good news and that is that in our estimates we are expecting inflation, even if nothing is done in the second half of the year, to decrease for reasons of seasonality, for structural reasons. The main shocks occurred previously, so now the base is high, it will grow a little less in the second half of the year. We would expect the inflation rate to moderate in the second half of the year. However, our country has previously managed to live with inflation of 8%, 7%, 10%, it is different from other countries that cannot live with it, we can live without major inconvenience. As I told you, higher prices mean more stimulus for production, so for a producer it is good, for a consumer not necessarily, so that is where the State has to design compensatory policies so that the cost and standard of living do not become too expensive. That is on the side of inflation. On the side of financial stability. We are already in a sustained stage of growth, in a full, consolidated stage of financial stability. And what we are observing is a financial system that remains robust, with adequate capital ratios, with adequate liquidity, with deposits growing, more than double-digit growth, and credit returning. In my last presentation I had pointed out that credit was difficult for him to return because, indeed, he timidly reared his head. That is no longer the case. Now credit has returned and that opens up opportunities for everyone TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION So, we have a financial system that is flowing, a stable exchange market, a mortgage market that is recovering. Interest rates in general, the interest rate on treasury bonds, the interest rate on deposits and credit, have been falling. This decline could probably be stopped by the rise in international prices, but it is a good time now to access financing. Insurance companies have increased insurance premiums. Insurance coverage and the stock market have also maintained their dynamism. In other words, we have a flowing financial market and an economy with the capacity to respond to external shocks. That's in terms of financial stability. And as for the external components of our economy. Yesterday when we published the balance of payments, it can be seen how in the first quarter, given the economic recovery, imports have grown more than exports, exports continue with their dynamism, but imports have responded more. There is a price effect there, from what we mentioned, inflation is being imported, it is clear, but the country is able to cover it. But, there is also a quantity effect and, in effect, quantity has also increased the volume of imports and exports. On the other hand, it is noteworthy in the balance of payments report that tourism is returning. Last year, the total amount of tourism, which had fallen sharply due to the pandemic, obtained revenues of around 180 million dollars, and only in this first quarter 110 million dollars in tourism revenues were already recorded. In other words, if we make a prospective we can reach no less than 400 million dollars. In other words, there is a good element of tourism that is observed in the statistics of services, mainly in the area of hotels and restaurants that are growing, are becoming more dynamic and we think that it will be more dynamic for this reason. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Remittances continue their dynamics. More than 600 million dollars in remittance income. I think that this is another important change that is happening post-pandemic that is widespread throughout Central America, Mexico, the Dominican Republic, which are the main countries that receive remittances from abroad, they are an important source of financing for the global economy and it is on the rise, that is a reality. That will continue and that will also continue to pay off in the growth of spending. That is what we observe on the side of the external sector. The dynamics of the external sector are also maintained, which, as I mentioned, has allowed the accumulation of reserves and has facilitated the exchange rate stability of our country. In perspective, then, we believe that the year 2022, the year in which we find ourselves, is going to be a year of economic growth for Nicaragua, lower than last year, which was more than 10%, but at natural trend rates that characterize our country, which could be, as I told you, between 4% and 5%. A lot will depend on what happens abroad, because our economy is well tied to world trade. There are dark clouds out there and these are the risks of a potential recession. We are oblivious at this time to that recession. But if it happens, well, we'll see. Because as I told you, the primary sector is very strong in Nicaragua, today it is very strong and has been able to adapt. The search for new markets could be a way out of the decline in trade. But, the truth, and what it has shown in the last four years, is that we have been able to resist and grow our exports. So, we see that exports are also going to continue to grow. Inflation that will fall in the second half of the year, but will perhaps be similar or a little less than last year. But it does continue to be an issue that will be addressed with the current mechanisms that are being addressed, but above all that will depend on what happens in the rest of the world. We see employment as well, which will continue to recover, the unemployment rate will most likely be at the current levels and stay there between 3.5 and 4%, we see no reason for it to fall further. And if conditions allow: a TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION For the years that follow, well, there we have to take out the glass ball a little. One can put wonders on paper, I think it has happened to you when you make your estimates, that on paper you can project three, four or five years and you see it wonderful or you see it badly, and the opposite comes out when you arrive. But the truth is that, if this trend continues, we should hope that the projection of economic growth and development in our country can be sustained without major trauma and that we can achieve the poverty reduction objectives that we have been setting for ourselves over the years, which has been the policy or the fundamental objective of all Nicaragua's macroeconomic policy. The Ministry of Finance has been working on seeking financing, building programs, building resilient mechanisms in the face of climate change, and now in the face of the issue of energy that was correctly mentioned here, which is one of the issues that will give everyone food for thought in the future, the mobilization towards alternative energy sources that allow us to sustain this economic growth. but that we believe that as a nation and as good Nicaraguans we will be able to confront them and we will emerge winners from this entire international environment and our national economy. Title: Nicaragua Economic Forum Development, impact of COVID-19 and economic outlook Ovidio Reyes Ramrez, President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua
text: ''faemfya/de Issuing confidence and stability Wednesday, March 16, 2022 Nicaragua Economic Forum Development, impact of COVID-19 and economic prospects Ovidio Reyes Ramirez, President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua Good morning to all of you present. Congratulations to CABEI for this beautiful building. Congratulations Dr. Mossi, to you and your entire team for having promoted this initiative. Dear Executive President of the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (CABEI), Mr. Dante Mossi; Minister of Finance and Public Credit, Ivan Acosta; Director for Nicaragua at CABEI, Uriel Perez; representatives of organizations, public officials, press team, all invited to this event. I would like to thank the Central American Bank for Economic Integration for the invitation to participate in the Economic Forum: "Development, Impact of COVID-19 and Economic Prospects" and especially for the kind invitation of Mr. Mossi, and congratulate you on the inauguration of this magnificent building that I am sure will host ideas, plans and projects for the development of our country. I think it is important to organize this Forum in the current post-pandemic context, in order to evaluate our progress and future challenges. After Minister Acosta's presentation on Nicaragua's National Development Plan, in which he highlighted the government's strategic priorities in the medium and long term, particularly in operationalizing public policy instruments aimed at promoting economic growth, reducing inequality and overcoming poverty, it is my turn to present Nicaragua's macroeconomic situation and its prospects in the short term. Thus, in my speech I will first present preliminary information for the year 2021, we will see how various indicators indicate a good dynamism in the first months of 2022 and how the Central Bank expects to continue supporting the economic recovery, and I will conclude by presenting the projections of the main macroeconomic variables for the year 2022, pointing out some challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in the short and medium term.  In what follows, I will present preliminary information on the different macroeconomic balances for the year 2021, inviting you to consult the 2021 Annual Report of the Central Bank of Nicaragua that we hope will be published at the end of this month, where you will find more detailed information and possibly with updates in some sectoral indicators.  2021 was a year of economic recovery and the return of growth of the Nicaraguan economy, after it was affected by various shocks since 2018 and the COVID-19 pandemic at the beginning of 2020. The pandemic generated tension on the economy throughout the year, but the improvement in the expectations of economic agents due to the progress of vaccination, the effective response of public policies and the constant promotion of production had a positive effect on economic activity in 2021. In this context, the domestic economy entered the expansion stage of the recovery process, registering a generalized growth of most activities, but still heterogeneous at the sectoral level. Preliminary estimates that we are releasing today indicate that the cumulative growth of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during 2021 will be around 10.3 percent, being -2% in 2020. By sector, the IMAE reflects that the sectors with the highest accumulated growth during the year were mining and quarrying (40.0%), construction (35.5%), commerce (16.1%), manufacturing industry (13.7%) and Hotels and Restaurants (10.5%). From the point of view of aggregate demand, the main impulse came from consumption and investment. Exports also increased, supported by a resurgence in external demand and better international prices, and consequently imports also increased. Regarding the boost in production in 2021, I would like to highlight two things, the first is that this dynamism was not observed only in Nicaragua, but was a homogeneous characteristic in the performance of Central American countries, as indicated in the recent press release of the Central American Monetary Council. The second is that, in the case of our country, the favorable The performance resulted in a level of economic activity similar to that observed in the first quarter of 2011 8.  As a result of this economic growth, the unemployment rate fell in the third quarter to 4.3 percent, according to the Continuous Household Survey (ECH) published by INIDE. However, this behavior reflects employment lags in relation to economic activity, as a result of an apparent recomposition in the labor market (between labor supply and demand). This generalized recomposition at the global level has been an effect of the pandemic, caused in part by the risks of COVID-1 contagion 9, which has led to a reduction in labor participation and new forms of (remote) work. Thus, towards the end of 2021, the global labor participation rate remained below its pre-pandemic level, indicating that the labor market has not yet completed its adjustment, both in supply and demand. On the other hand, formal employment measured by affiliation to the Nicaraguan Social Security Institute (INSS) increased by 46,748 contributors during 2021, registering an increase of 6.5 percent compared to December 2020.  The dynamism of economic activity developed in a context of inflationary pressures, the effect of which was transferred to the Nicaraguan economy. Indeed, the recovery of the global economy and fiscal and monetary stimulus policies boosted external demand and global spending in 2021, leading to higher prices globally, including a broad-based increase in commodity prices (mainly energy and fuels), exacerbated by supply chain difficulties and the emergence of new variants of COVID-19. As a result of these factors, national inflation reached 7.21 percent in 2021, when it was 2.93 percent in 2020, in correspondence with the evolution of external prices. In terms of contribution to year-on-year inflation, the largest impulses came from the food and non-alcoholic beverages, transportation, and accommodation and utilities divisions (which totaled 5.15 p.p.). Core inflation, which isolates the most volatile goods from the basket of goods with which the CPI is calculated, increased, standing at 5.45 percent. It should be noted that the policy of reducing the rate of exchange rate slippage that was implemented in 20199 and in 2020, when it was reduced from 5 to 3 percent at first, and to 2 percent at a later stage, together with the continuity of the policy of targeted subsidies on the part of the Government, avoided greater pressures on domestic prices.  With regard to public finances, economic growth and the better expectations of economic agents improved the performance of fiscal indicators, while the continuity of a prudent and active fiscal policy was observed in obtaining resources to guarantee basic social services and investment and infrastructure. In this regard, the Central Government's tax collection improved substantially by growing 26.5 percent, supported by the dynamism of economic activity, while public spending increased, prioritizing social spending on health and guaranteeing the resources to promote the Public Investment Program (PIP). Consequently, the deficit of the Non-Financial Public Sector (NFPS) was reduced to 1.5 percent of GDP in 2021 versus 2.5 percent in 2020. Likewise, public debt was reduced to 64.2 percent of GDP versus 64.8 percent in 2020 and maintained sustainable levels. This contrasts with what has been observed in most economies that had increased their public deficits and increased their public debt. The history of responsible fiscal performance and the active management of financial resources resulted in the obtaining of flows of concessional external loans and placements of Bonds of the Republic of Nicaragua (BRN) at lower rates of return than in previous years, thus allowing the sound financing of the public deficit.  The global economic recovery favored external flows, in particular the evolution of exports, flows of family remittances, and foreign direct investment (FDI), among others. Thus, merchandise exports increased by 23.1 percent (5.8% in 2020), driven mainly by the manufacturing and mining sector, and with an increase in the volume exported (mainly gold, live cattle, peanuts, among others) and international prices (mainly beef, sugar, coffee, among others). Exports from free zones grew by 36.8 percent, when they fell 14.7% in 2020, boosted by the recovery of global demand that favored the textiles, harnesses and tobacco branches.  Household remittance flows increased by 10% (in 2020), driven mainly by income from growing economies (the US and Spain). Foreign direct investment showed a recovery trend, with flows mainly directed to the energy and mining and telecommunications sectors. In turn, tourism revenues reflected recovery at the quarter-on-quarter level, although in the aggregate of the year decreased 7.4 percent compared to 2020, when they fell 61.5 percent in 2020, due to the continuity of restrictions associated with the pandemic.  At the same time, domestic economic growth boosted the growth of import volumes, which also increased in value due to the effect of high international inflation, and, in particular, due to the increase in the price of oil and derivatives, resulting in a deterioration in the terms of trade, equivalent to 5.2 percent (import prices increased by 1 1.7 percent and export prices by 5.9 percent). As a result, imports of FOB merchandise increased by 37.3 percent, which led to an increase in the merchandise trade deficit of 63.3 percent compared to the deficit observed in 2020. The largest year-on-year increases in imports by destination were observed in the oil bill (64%), capital goods (56.2%) and intermediate goods (36.2%).  Monetary and financial variables improved their performance. Thus, monetary aggregates continued to reflect positive double-digit year-on-year rates of change and the foreign exchange market remained stable, with results of net purchases of foreign currency by the Central Bank of Nicaragua and the financial system. On the other hand, the provision of monetary instruments by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which facilitated the management of liquidity in the financial system in national and foreign currency, fiscal prudence in a context of growth in tax collection, which facilitated transfers of resources to the Central Bank of Nicaragua, and the increase in external flows, which favored the supply of foreign currency, contributed to the accumulation of international reserves and the absence of exchange rate pressures in that market. Thus, the exchange rate gap for sales was below the foreign exchange sales commission charged by the Central Bank of Nicaragua. 1 1. As a result, Gross International Reserves reached a balance of 4,046.6 million dollars at the end of 2021, which represented an increase of 834.7 million dollars compared to 2020 and the equivalent of a coverage of 2.8 times the monetary base, an adequate level that sustains the stability of the current exchange rate regime.  At the same time, financial intermediation continued to consolidate, with deposits and credit growing at positive rates. Thus, the gross loan portfolio grew 4.9 percent and deposits 12 percent. The consolidation of financial stability was partly the result of the greater dynamism of economic activity, which had a positive impact on the expectations of economic agents and the ability of households and companies to pay. However, although credit grew, it continues to lag behind the dynamics of economic activity, so that the increase in bank liquidity resulting from the increase in deposits was channeled in part to investments in public securities, both by the Central Bank of Nicaragua and by the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit.  The banking system and financial institutions maintained a solid and resilient position, showing stability in funding sources, and capital and liquidity levels comfortably complying with regulatory minimums. Thus, the indicator of availabilities on obligations was 45.3 percent. Likewise, the reactivation of credit was also reflected in improvements in the quality of the portfolio, observing a reduction in the non-performing loan portfolio and in judicial collection, which stood at 2.4 percent of the gross portfolio, when this was 4.1 percent at the end of 2020.  Recent macroeconomic indicators indicate that the good economic performance of 2021 continues to be maintained in the first months of 2022, consolidating in a phase of relatively solid growth.  In this sense, formal employment has continued to grow; the inflow of external resources in the form of family remittances and merchandise exports persists; intermediation continues to recover through the growth of credit and deposits; financing flows to the Non-Financial Public Sector are maintained; the exchange market remains stable; and international reserves have strengthened and continue to grow. However, inflationary pressures from abroad also persist. In this context, the BCN has kept the Reference Rate of Monetary Repos stable at 3.5 percent in the first months of the year, but it is most likely that it will begin to readjust its monetary policy in correspondence with what is happening in the rest of the economies.  The Central Bank will continue to support exchange rate stability and financial intermediation. On the side of exchange rate policy, the lincations of the 2022 Monetary Program establish the maintenance of the sliding rate with respect to the U.S. dollar at 2% per year and the convertibility of the national currency to the established exchange rate, through the exchange desk. On the monetary policy side, the Central Bank will continue to ensure adequate coverage of gross international reserves to support the exchange rate (equivalent to 2.7 times the monetary base), promote the reactivation of financial intermediation and favor the liquidity of the financial system through the various monetary policy instruments. However, the Central Bank will maintain vigilance to react accordingly to the expected increases in international interest rates. 1 7. Finally, the Central Bank projects that the Nicaraguan economy will grow in 2022 in a range of between 4.0 - 5.0 percent, mainly supported by the expansion of private investment and exports. This growth is expected to be led mainly by construction, trade and manufacturing activities. As well as by the greater external demand. In the case of inflation, the Central Bank expects it to be in a range of between 5.0 - 6.0 percent by the end of 2022, expecting the year-on-year rate to increase slightly towards the end of June for the most part, due to the pass-through of international prices to domestic prices, but that it will be reduced during the second half of 2022. The non-financial public sector deficit in 2022 is also projected to be around 2 percent of GDP and the current account of the balance of payments is projected to end with a deficit of 2.4 percent of GDP, due to higher imports of goods associated with the economic recovery and the increase in oil prices. 18. The macroeconomic context for the country in 2022 is exposed to challenges due to the global context of uncertainty, but opportunities were also identified. On the challenge side, fears persist of the emergence of COVID-1 9 variants that could prolong disruptions in global supply chains; there are concerns that geopolitical tensions may result in the persistence of rising oil and other commodity prices, which poses inflationary risks and impacts that would affect supply and demand globally; and additionally there is uncertainty about the effects of the expected tightening of international monetary policy. On the opportunity side, higher external demand for food is expected to continue and international price increases are expected to favor domestic exports of primary goods. Likewise, Nicaragua could take advantage of strategies such as nearshoring, or bringing value chains closer together, which could be attractive to the country, which could lead to greater foreign direct investment, exports and job creation. So much for my presentation. And, to conclude, I would like to reiterate my gratitude to CABEI and Mr. Mossi for their kind invitation to this event and congratulate them again for this building that stands as a sign of CABEI's continued institutional commitment to be a strategic partner for Nicaragua. Thanks a lot.

Por el lado de la poltica monetaria, el Banco Central continuar GerenciadeComunicaciones@bcn.gob.ni www.bcn.gob.ni facebook tujitter^ asegurando una cobertura adecuada de las reservas internacionales brutas que soporte al tipo de cambio (equivalente a 2.7 veces la base monetaria), propiciar la reactivacin de la intermediacin financiera y favorecer la liquidez del sistema financiero a travs de los diversos instrumentos de poltica monetaria. No obstante, el Banco Central mantendr la vigilancia para reaccionar en correspondencia a las alzas esperadas de las tasas de inters internacionales. 1 7. Finalmente, el Banco Central proyecta que la economa nicaragense crecer en 2022 en un rango de entre 4.0 - 5.0 por ciento, sustentado principalmente en la expansin de la inversin privada y de las exportaciones. Se espera que este crecimiento sea liderado principalmente por las actividades de construccin, comercio e industria manufacturera. As como tambin, por la mayor demanda externa. En el caso de la inflacin, el Banco Central prev que esta se ubique en un rango de entre 5.0 - 6.0 por ciento hacia fines de 2022, esperando que la tasa interanual aumente ligeramente hacia fines de junio en su mayor parte, debido al traspaso de los precios internacionales a los precios domsticos, pero que se reducir durante el segundo semestre de 2022. Tambin se proyecta que el dficit del sector pblico no financiero en 2022 se ubique en alrededor del 2 por ciento del PIB y que la cuenta corriente de la balanza de pagos finalice con un dficit de 2.4 por ciento del PIB, por mayores importaciones de mercancas asociadas a la recuperacin econmica y el aumento de los precios del petrleo. 18. El contexto macroeconmico para el pas en 2022 est expuesto a retos debido al contexto global de incertidumbre, pero tambin se identificaron oportunidades. Por el lado de los retos, persisten los temores de surgimiento de variantes de COVID-1 9 que podran prolongar las interrupciones en las cadenas globales de suministros; existen preocupaciones porque las tensiones geopolticas puedan resultar en la persistencia en el aumento de los precios del petrleo y otras materias primas, lo que plantea riesgos inflacionarios e impactos que afectaran la oferta y demanda a nivel global; y adicionalmente hay incertidumbre sobre los efectos del endurecimiento esperado de la poltica monetaria internacional. Por el lado de las oportunidades, se espera que contine una mayor demanda externa de alimentos y que los aumentos de precios internacionales favorezcan las exportaciones nacionales de bienes primarios. Asimismo, Nicaragua podra aprovechar estrategias como la del nearshoring, o de acercamiento de las cadenas de valor, que pudiesen resultar atractivos al pas, lo que pudiera derivar en una mayor inversin extranjera directa, exportaciones y generacin de empleo. Hasta aqu mi presentacin. Y, para finalizar, quisiera reiterar mi agradecimiento al BCIE y al Sr. Mossi por su amable invitacin a este evento y felicitarlos nuevamente por este edificio que se erige como muestra del continuo compromiso institucional del BCIE de ser un socio estratgico para Nicaragua. Title: Press Conference Report on the Results of the Meeting of the National System of Production, Consumption and Trade President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R.
text: TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Issuing confidence and stability Issuing confidence and stability Press Conference Report on the Results of the National System of Production, Consumption and Trade Meeting President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. November 10, 2023 President of the BCN: Good morning! September 29, 2023 President of the BCN: Good morning. We are going to explain the issues addressed today at the meeting held every Friday by various State institutions, known as the National System of Production, Consumption and Trade, where we evaluate the goals, progress of production and the policies that are implemented for such an important task of national interest. Today we saw the evaluation of the goals of the Production System, the progress that the plan has made to date. We also evaluated a report on fisheries and aquaculture, how the progress of their exports is and the implementation of the National Strategy for the Promotion of Small-Scale Aquaculture. We also saw the monitoring of the Precious Grains, Coffee and Cocoa Strategy, and, finally, we talked about the evolution of prices. Then I will summarize the issues addressed there. First, we saw the progress of production. We observe, for example, that the Monthly Index of Economic Activity (IMAE), which measures national productive activity, in the month of July had a significant rebound presenting a growth of 5.9%. This rate is relevant because it indicates that the economy has not only passed the cyclical moments, but is on a path of growth, and what is already accumulating in relation to the IMAE is already a growth of 4.1%. This indicates that the third quarter is going to be a good quarter in terms of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) activity, as the first and second quarters already were. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Issuing confidence and stability Issuing confidence and stability Then, we saw what corresponds to the individual items that have to do with the different activities that are monitored. In particular, (agricultural) exports as of August are accumulating an amount of 2,138 million dollars, out of a goal that we expect to reach of 2,965 million dollars. In other words, we have already advanced by 72.1% and compared to the previous year we are growing by 1%. In this regard, the responses that we have observed in sectors that previously had been showing slightly less dynamic rates have been important. But also, the world is stabilizing prices and that has been a factor for exports to show a value of 1% growth. The important thing is that there is a dynamic and that it continues to expand. On the other hand, we observe that in the case of agro-exportable products, peanuts and tobacco are the ones that have been growing the most. The case of tobacco, for example, shows a growth of 19% from January to August, from 179 thousand quintals to 213 thousand quintals and in the case of peanuts, 1.5 million quintals; and last year 1.4 million quintals. In basic grains, bean exports continue at 1,513,000 quintals versus 1,454,000 quintals last year for a growth of TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Issuing confidence and stability Issuing confidence and stability In the case of fishing, which has had a cyclical element that has shown decelerating rates, a recovery is already observed in the case of scales and lobsters. For example, in scales, which are the known fish, 8.3 million pounds were exported versus 7.5 million pounds last year and in lobster 2.2 million pounds were exported versus 1.4 million pounds last year. This is in general what we observe in the evolution of the main export and global production products. We see a good dynamic and we predict a good result for this year. In the particular case, as we mentioned about fishing, we also analyzed all the products that have been made there, such as farmed shrimp, scales, pink conch, sea cucumbers, tuna, and the recovery of sea cucumber and lobster stands out in particular, for example, the landings of Caribbean lobsters of 3.3 million pounds in July-August 2023. In July-August 2022, these had been 2.5 million pounds, that is, there is a growth of 33%. And well, and all the activities of the fishing sector are also advancing there. How much do pond cultures represent? To give us an idea of its size, in the case of farmed shrimp, 41.5 million pounds are farmed TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Issuing confidence and stability Issuing confidence and stability So, that is what we have on the side of productive issues. Regarding the Price Strategy for Precious Beans, these have been receiving special attention because we are talking about coffee and cocoa. 31,360 producers have been served, which is 74% of the goal and this care is progressing at a good pace. 1,043 visits were also made to coffee farms for 2,866 trapping services and monitoring of seven pests, including the coffee borer. A total of 1,353 visits were also made to cocoa farms to monitor three pests and 269 soil and root analyses for coffee, and 152 soil and root analyses in cocoa for pest diagnosis. 6,325 protagonists have also been trained in coffee collection, quantifiable analysis methods to evaluate samples and artisanal chocolate production. The strategy also includes carrying out 25 experiments and established research, which have already been implemented by INTA colleagues for 19 and the strategy is moving forward with the intention of not only increasing the production of coffee and cocoa, but also improving their quality, which is carried out through special fairs and through the promotion of our coffee and cocoa. of our precious grains. We also addressed the issue of national avocado production, which is a new issue that is being incorporated into our plans. It was already being carried out, but now through specific production areas for the production of this good. There are 1,214 blocks already registered and that are being served, in Masaya 471 blocks, in Carazo 370 blocks, in Rivas 147 blocks, and then there are 226 blocks distributed in the rest of the departments. And here this is an avocado for export, a good part, and the other is destined for national consumption of the various varieties that exist and that are recorded, such as the Benick, Simpson, Choquette, Hass and other varieties that are demanded by the public and the population. The TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Issuing confidence and stability Issuing confidence and stability Finally, we monitored prices. The most important thing is that prices in the last three, four months have stopped accelerating. We are now in a stage of slowdown. Last year prices were more than 11% growth, this year they have 7.5% growth. (Domestic) prices are a result of international prices. Basically, what we have observed is an increase in costs, an increase in inputs for imported goods. However, there are good signs that some of these have already stabilized and that they will not continue to grow. As a result, inflation at the national level begins to stabilize and prices begin to stabilize. This is good news, since the last four months also in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) growth is very low and we would expect September to be the same. So, we see that prices have started to give way. In the year it has a growth of 7.5% and in the best case scenario this could end between 6 and 7% by the end of 2023 and by 2024 we would expect a firmer stabilization. So, in summary, we have good indicators on the productive side. The economy is advancing in expansion, with growth in July of 5.9%, July versus July 2022, and in the accumulated of 4.1%. We have already overcome the cyclical moments of the economy and we would now expect to enter this stage of sustained growth and the indicators also by items and the strategies and plans that are being developed give us a glimpse of it. Title: Interview of the President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R., with the Journalist Oscar Morales of the program La Notificacin, Channel 8
text: TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Interview with the President of the BCN, Ovidio ReyesTN8 Notification Program January 1, 2023 Journalist Oscar Morales Nicaragua resumed the path of growth and since January 1 the indicators reveal that there is growth, the engines of these impulses have been the economic policies meticulously elaborated to return to this trend that the country had since 2007. How are we doing to date? Are we prepared to face any other challenge? This is what the authorities tell us. Thank you and welcome to a new interview here on your program, La Notificacion de TN 8, the economic close of the year 2022 is news. We spoke exclusively and in depth about this subject, our special guest, the President of the Central Bank of Nicaragua, Ovidio Reyes, is with us, to whom we thank for having attended this invitation. Journalist Oscar Morales We begin by asking you: How does the country's economy close in 2022, President? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. facebook I hujitter facebook I hujitter Tube Tube TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. There are good economic policies. There is the formulation of a fairly strong fiscal program in terms of continuity of investment and infrastructure spending and social spending, and with a fairly significant recovery in revenue that has allowed these resources to be funded. The impetus for fiscal policy has been important. On the other hand, we also have a monetary policy in balance that maintains a good composition in the money market and interest rates that remain quite stable, both in the deposit portfolio and in the rest of the financial instruments. And on the other hand, we have a strong dynamism of productive, entrepreneurial and business activity that has motivated us to have booming exports, with a lot of dynamism and a flow of income from tourism, foreign investment also growing. Mr. President, did foreign direct investment grow in 2022? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. It is rebuilding in amounts of more than 1,000 million dollars per year. In fact, this first semester we already reached that amount of investment and we believe that it will continue in the following years. Investment that comes from both companies since they are in the country and new ventures and the areas are fundamentally the production sector, in the primary sector of the economy, mining, in the sector also of the Free Trade Zone the dynamism and continuity of investment is observed and in the rest of the sector of energy activity and infrastructure. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. Well, the export sector as such did not have a depression, rather what it had was a slowdown due to issues of the Covid pandemic that generated obstacles in international trade. Once these obstacles were overcome and productive activity returned, then exports continued to grow. In fact, in all these years exports have only shown growth and the sectors that were affected by the pandemic were the services sector, trade and tourism, which, however, are already recovering again. Has employment been recovering in 2022? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. Employment suffered a lot with the pandemic. Because the pandemic led many families to make the decision to stay at home to avoid contagion, and many jobs that used to be provided with contact, are now no longer done that way, electronic means and couriers are used. So, that has changed the dynamics of employment in the world, not only in Nicaragua. However, after the worst moment of the pandemic passed, employment has been recovering strongly, formal employment, such as those insured by the INSS, almost 800 thousand people are already employed and the unemployment rate has dropped significantly. The unemployment rate is currently around 3.3%. So, there has been a recovery in economic activity and also in employment, which is the most important thing. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. The country has many strengths and with the pandemic these strengths emerged. First, entrepreneurship was a great strength. Some mention the informal activity sector as something negative, but this sector really allowed to cushion much of the employment that was lost on the formal side. So that was a determining factor. And on the other hand, we also have, as I mentioned, the dynamism of exports as one of the great strengths that this country has, and that strength is what allows us to reach figures in the order of more than 7 billion dollars at this time. So, we believe that those strengths are going to come to light at any other negative moment. The country then appeals and consolidates its strengths, which are on the side of production. And on the other hand, we have a fiscal policy that has huge revenues, a tax reform that was implemented and that left the country in a better position. How much is the monetary base today, President? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. The monetary base is in the order of 40 billion cordobas, more or less. It goes up a lot in this December season, then it goes down, it has seasonality, we call it in economics, but on average it is more or less located in the order of 40 billion cordobas. What the Central Bank does is inject healthy money into the economy, supported by reserves so that monetary and exchange rate balance is maintained. Journalist Oscar Morales And how is the financial system and deposits doing in 2022? Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION The most important thing that happened in 2022 is that credit returned to the economy, remained depressed for a long time, quite timid I would say, and then obtained a significant rebound starting in March of this year and is now growing at significant rates. So, we believe that credit growth will be a determining factor in what will be the subsequent consolidation of the economic recovery during 2023 and deposits have not stopped growing. In fact, they had a slight drop during the shock, but in the pandemic they recovered strongly. Are you working to make credit easier, President? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. What the government has always promoted on the side of the Public Treasury is the search for external financing to support credit programs and that has indeed been achieved. Also the search for financing through international organizations to support production. On the side of the Central Bank, what we have done is to facilitate liquidity, to create instruments for monetary repurchases, for investments here at the Central Bank, which serve as alternatives to banking, and all this has worked in a well-coordinated way in such a way that funding is guaranteed for banking activity and private banks have also found sources of external financing. in addition to their own, which are the deposits. We want to ask you, what behavior did the country's economy have with the delivery of the 2022 Christmas bonus? TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Journalist Oscar Morales Well, the Christmas bonus is an important push factor, since it means one month's salary for all workers during these festive seasons and we believe that credit, commerce, above all, are benefiting a lot from this activity of the Christmas bonus, which is a little more than 13 billion cordobas, it is a very strong boost and also because the public sector, as the rains are over, it also gives it a boost through the Adelante program. And what do the risk rating agencies say, has Nicaragua been improving its position? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. The rating agencies have been improving their evaluation of our country. We have talked to all of them. At least one has already made an improvement in Nicaragua's rating and we would expect the others to also come in the same direction. Recently, the Monetary Fund also had the opportunity to visit our country and make a macroeconomic assessment that was positive for the economy as a whole, and we believe that this reality of economic recovery will also be reflected in all the evaluations that come. And in economic terms, what does 2023 look like? President of the BCN, Ovidio Reyes R. 2023 is seen as a year at the international level with difficulties, at the international level, because economies expect to slow down in 2023, because the world is still being subjected to disturbances, the markets are not yet stabilized. The oil market is not yet in long-term equilibrium. The energies in general are not in a good position and so they are TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION We expect the economy to be fully accommodated in 2023, after we had a spectacular growth of more than 10% during 2021. So, this year we would now be accommodating ourselves to a growth that is going to be between 3.5% and 4.5%, 4% on average. And next year we would expect that growth, due to these international factors for our country, to be between 3% and 4%, because our countries benefit a lot because they are very small countries in international trade. Even though global trade may be going down, that is not necessarily the case for us, because our products, being relative to the world, small in quantity, are easily accommodated and sell quickly. A country that sells a lot and that there is a global recession is different, it affects it a lot. This is not our case, so we would believe that the economy would grow between 3% and 4% next year. Inflation was the international factor that had the greatest impact this year and we could end up between 10% and 11% this year, but we would expect that next year it will be between 5% and 6%. And the basis for this is that the prices of international goods have already stopped growing and the price of oil itself has fallen a little after the significant increase it had at the beginning of the year. So, as prices have already stopped growing, international prices, we believe that this will also translate into lower inflation during 2023 and would be between 5% and 6%. And employment, we believe that an employment rate between 3 and 3.5% will be maintained, * both this year and next, and we see a strengthening of the growth of the formal sector, employment, the economy and a slight reduction in informality, that is what the statistics at the end of 2022 are telling us and we hope that this will continue during 2023. And so we end, we thank you once again for heeding this invitation and sharing these projections of what is expected for the coming year, and to you families, we thank you for the privilege of your time. TRANSCRIPTION TRANSCRIPTION of Issuing confidence and stability *Explanatory note: The range of between 3 and 3.5% corresponds to the projected unemployment rate for 2022 and 2023.
